processing: Medium oxidation, strip-rolled and roasted, traditionally medium to heavy over charcoal, by the same general method as Wuyi rock tea but from larger, gentler gardens; export grades are machine-roasted and blended.
harvest_season: Spring (late April to May), with a smaller autumn picking in some gardens; spring is the quality harvest.
appearance_dry: Long, loosely twisted, broad dark strips, a little less tight and more varied than Wuyi Shui Xian.
appearance_wet: Large, thick, broad olive-brown leaves with red edges.
taste_profile: Roasted sweetness, honey and a soft orchid-narcissus note on a smooth, medium-full body, with less mineral grip and a shorter finish than Wuyi Shui Xian; old-garden lots add a woody, mossy depth.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, gaiwan or zisha pot, short early steeps. It is forgiving of long steeps and makes a good pot tea too: 5 g per 300 ml, 2 minutes, three times.

vintage_note: Spring harvest of the current year, roasted over the summer and sold from autumn with the year stated, like Wuyi tea but at lower prices; medium and heavy roasts keep three to five years and old lots are sold aged with the vintage. Export Shui Hsien in tins is blended and sold without a vintage.
description:
Minbei Shui Xian is Shui Xian from its home ground: the hills of Jianyang and Jianou in northern Fujian, just outside the Wuyi scenic area, where the cultivar was first found and where much of the world's Shui Xian is grown. It is the honest, affordable version of a tea whose Wuyi cousin carries a premium for the name on the mountain.

The cultivar was identified in Jianyang in the nineteenth century, by tradition in the Daoguang reign beside a cave near Zhudun village, and spread from there into Wuyi and south to Zhangping and Yongchun. Jianou has an even older tea pedigree, as the home of the imperial Beiyuan gardens that made pressed tribute tea in the Song dynasty, but what it produces today is roasted strip oolong, and a lot of it. Chinese tea standards and the trade treat Minbei Shui Xian as a category of its own, separate from Wuyi Shui Xian, which is sold as rock tea.

It is made by the same route as yancha: mature leaf, overnight shaking to a medium oxidation, strip rolling and a charcoal or electric roast, usually medium to heavy. The gardens are larger and the soil is deeper and less rocky, which shows in the cup: plenty of roasted sweetness, honey and the cultivar's orchid note, a smooth body, but less of the mineral grip and the long cooling aftertaste of the best Wuyi lots. Old gardens in Shuiji produce lao cong Shui Xian with a woody depth that rivals Wuyi's at a fraction of the price.

Brew it hot with a full gaiwan or in a pot; it is forgiving and makes a comforting everyday roasted oolong, and it is the leaf behind the Shui Hsien tins that Fujian has exported to Southeast Asia and Europe for generations.

Sold by the current spring harvest with the roast year, or in blended export tins without one, it keeps for years if the roast is medium or heavier and takes well to ageing. When buying, look for long, intact strips and a sweet rather than acrid roast; ask whether the tea is from old bushes; and if a shop prices a Minbei Shui Xian like a zhengyan Wuyi tea, walk on.
sources_note: The Beiyuan tribute-tea history of Jianou is well documented; the separate trade categorisation of Minbei versus Wuyi Shui Xian follows Chinese standards and vendor practice.
history:
Shui Xian belongs to northern Fujian. The Jianyang county gazetteer, as usually quoted, dates the plant to the Daoguang reign of the Qing, when a grower found it by a cave mouth on a hill at Zhudun village. The name is said to come from the local pronunciation of Zhu, which sounds like Shui. Old bushes shown as the mother trees stand at Dahu village in Xiaohu town, marked by a stone from 1988.

Jianou keeps old plantings too, including a tree at Lukou in Nanya that one account also calls a mother tree.
